content: Systolic hypertension is characterized by an elevated systolic blood pressure while the diastolic blood pressure remains within the normal range. This condition is often attributed to reduced compliance of the aorta, which becomes more pronounced with advancing age. Several randomized controlled trials have demonstrated the benefits of treating systolic hypertension. SHEP Study The SHEP (Systolic Hypertension in the Elderly Program) study was a randomized controlled trial that showed a reduction of three strokes per 100 patients treated over a five-year period. Patient Inclusion Criteria: Systolic blood pressure (SBP) between 160 and 219 mm Hg, and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) less than 90 mm Hg. Exclusion Criteria: Patients with a history of stroke accompanied by residual paresis or other neurological disabilities were excluded. Baseline Blood Pressure: The mean initial blood pressure was 170/77 mm Hg. Treatment Goal: The aim was to reduce sitting systolic blood pressure by at least 20 mm Hg or to achieve a target of less than 150 mm Hg. Results: The mean final blood pressure in the treatment group was 151/79 mm Hg, with 44% of patients achieving the target blood pressure. HYVET Trial The HYVET (Hypertension in the Very Elderly Trial) study, while not specifically labeled as a trial for systolic hypertension, included a subgroup of patients aged 80 years or older who predominantly had systolic hypertension. Patient Inclusion Criteria: SBP greater than 160 mm Hg. Baseline Blood Pressure: The mean baseline blood pressure was 173/91 mm Hg. Treatment Goal: The target blood pressure was 150/80 mm Hg. Results: The mean final blood pressure in the treatment group was not explicitly reported, but differences between the treatment and control groups were noted. SPRINT Trial The SPRINT (Systolic Blood Pressure Intervention Trial) study, though not specifically a trial of systolic hypertension, included a subgroup of patients aged 75 years or older with hypertension but without diabetes. Patient Inclusion Criteria: Patients aged 75 years or older with hypertension. Exclusion Criteria: Patients with a history of stroke or an SBP of less than 110 mm Hg after one minute of standing were excluded. Baseline Blood Pressure: The mean baseline blood pressure was 142/71 mm Hg. Treatment Goal: The study compared two treatment targets: an intensive target of less than 120 mm Hg and a standard target of less than 140 mm Hg. Results: The mean final blood pressure in the intensive treatment group was 123/63 mm Hg, while the mean final blood pressure in the control group was 135/67 mm Hg. Treatment Goal Based on these studies, treating systolic hypertension to achieve a systolic blood pressure of 140 mm Hg appears to be safe, provided the diastolic blood pressure remains at or above 68 mm Hg. A meta-analysis of individual patient data from randomized controlled trials identified a nadir diastolic blood pressure of 85 mm Hg, below which cardiovascular outcomes worsen. This J-shaped curve may be explained by poor health conditions leading to low blood pressure and an increased risk of mortality. Interpreting the meta-analysis is challenging, but avoiding a diastolic blood pressure below 68–70 mm Hg seems prudent for the following reasons: 1. The nadir value of 85 mm Hg for treated hypertensive patients in the meta-analysis is higher than the 68–70 mm Hg nadir suggested by the two major randomized controlled trials of isolated systolic hypertension. 2. The two largest trials in the meta-analysis, the Hypertension Detection and Follow-up Program (HDFP) and the Medical Research Council trial in mild hypertension (MRC1), predominantly included middle-aged subjects, all of whom had diastolic hypertension prior to treatment.
